newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end slightly off ahead of new supply.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end slightly off ahead of new supply.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed slightly lower in thin trading as players were mostly sidelined ahead of the first leg of the Treasury's quarterly refunding effort on Tuesday, analysts said.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended off 1/32 at 97-10/32. Its yield was unchanged at 6.70 percent.

Analysts said the lack of fresh data on Monday prompted participants to adjust positions early in the session and then take a more cautious stance in the afternoon session ahead of the upcoming supply.

The Treasury will offer the market $39.75 billion at its refunding auctions this week. The sale will be made up of $17.75 billion in three-year notes on Tuesday, $12.0 billion in 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10.0 billion in 30-year bonds on Thursday.
Analysts said uncertainty about the future performance of the of U.S. dollar against other major currencies was another factor keeping investors on the sidelines on Monday.
The market's dollar concerns were triggered by remarks late last week by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin saying that "We've had a strong dollar for some time."

Rubin's remarks gained momentum after the Group of Seven industrialized nations (G-7) signaled unity in their desire to arrest the dollar's recent rise against major foreign currencies. The G-7 officials met last Saturday in Berlin.

"We didn't get any new data today to stir the market so we were just left wondering what it means that a further rise in the dollar is not desired by the G-7," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A Inc.
"This created an air of uncertainty, a lack of conviction to do a lot of buying ahead of the auction. But also a lack of conviction to aggressively shorten the market," he added.
Some traders said they noted some short-covering during the day when the dollar bounced from its overnight lows.
"There was some short-covering when the market turned positive for a little while. But the move was very short-lived," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
Analysts said the market will now be keeping a close eye on the performance of the dollar and how it might affect demand for the upcoming Treasury refunding effort.
"You probably will not get strong demand from the Japanese side because it doesn't look like there is a lot of further upside there," I.D.E.A.'s Stiles said.
The dollar closed Monday trading session in New York at 1.6578 mark and at 122.93 yen.
Analysts said the market remained mostly rangebound going into the auctions, adding the session on Monday shed little light on which direction the market will take next.
"It's kind of hard to forecast the market's direction based on today's activity," said Chris Rupkey, vice president at Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed up one basis point at 5.00 percent. The six-month bill rate rose one point to 5.06 percent.
The year bill rate was up two points at 5.21 percent.

The two-year note closed down 1/32 at 100-1/32, yielding 5.86 percent. The five-year note traded off 1/32 at 100-13/32 to yield 6.15 percent. The ten-year note closed down 1/32 at 100-22/32, yielding 6.40 percent.
